text: A condition that lasts for years does not present a single moment to be diagnosed.
Arthur Kleinman, whose work is read far outside medicine, made the point differently.
A patient whose testimony is dismissed stops offering one.
Narrative medicine, which grew out of clinical practice, is not literary theory.
The account she gives is itself evidence.
This is a condition which has no cure, only management.
Kleinman, whose work I keep returning to, puts it differently.
The people who carry most of this are the caregivers.
A testimony that is dismissed is a testimony that stops being offered.

I trained as a physician and I still think the most useful forty minutes of my week are the ones I spend not treating anybody. I sit with someone who has been ill for a long time and I ask them to tell me how it started, and I do not interrupt. What comes back is almost never a list of symptoms. It is a story about a job that had to be given up, a marriage that reorganized itself around appointments, a mother who moved in. Colleagues tell me that this is lovely but that it is not medicine. My answer is that I have changed treatment plans because of what came out in those forty minutes, and I have never once changed a plan because of a tidier list of symptoms. The story is where the information about adherence lives. If you do not know what a person is protecting, you cannot know what they will and will not do at home.

My wife has been ill for eleven years, so I have been a caregiver for eleven years, and nobody has ever used that word to my face in a hospital. I am the person who remembers the medication schedule, the person who notices the day before a bad week starts, and the person who is standing in the corridor while the conversation that decides everything happens on the other side of a door. What I would say to any clinician listening to this is very simple. Ask me what I have seen. I am not asking to be included out of politeness. I have eleven years of observation that is not in your file, and most of the time nobody has ever asked for it. When somebody finally does ask, it takes ninety seconds and it changes what they decide.
A condition that lasts for years is called chronic.
The clinician who listened for forty minutes changed the plan.
Kleinman, whose work I keep returning to, is an anthropologist.
Narrative medicine, which grew out of clinical practice, is not literary theory.
A patient whose testimony is dismissed stops offering one.
Empathy is a skill that can be trained.
The account she gives is itself evidence.
This is a condition which has no cure, only management.
Kleinman, whose work I keep returning to, puts it differently.
The people who carry most of this are the caregivers.
A testimony that is dismissed is a testimony that stops being offered.
